In BEVFusion's released code, however, the 20 epochs train the lidar-only detector, and the camera + lidar model is then trained from that checkpoint for 6 epochs, the number Fusion4CA reports for itself [P, BEVFusion repository]. edits.old: SGO times can also be imprecise: the Rimrock record gives 00:03, while the ODI resume dates the fatal crash to 28 Nov 2023.
edits.new: Tesla files its SGO times in UTC (coordinated universal time), not local time: in the 2021–25 archive, the lighting field of 97% of the 1,563 Tesla reports that give a time and a lighting condition agrees with that time read as UTC, against 49% read as local time, whereas the 217 such reports from all other companies agree with local time (93%) and not with UTC (50%) [E: mid-month solar elevation at each state's centre]. The Rimrock record (13781-8004) shows the effect. It gives only the month, November 2023, with 00:03 and the lighting "Dawn / Dusk"; the ODI resume dates the fatal crash to 28 Nov 2023, and the Arizona Department of Public Safety placed it just after 5 p.m. on 27 Nov [P; T, AP via CBS News, 18 Oct 2024]. Both fit a crash at 17:03 on 27 Nov, because Arizona keeps UTC−7 all year and 17:03 there is 00:03 UTC on 28 Nov [E]. The time is therefore omitted from the table, and the other times shown are as filed; in local time they are 14:19 or 15:19 (Red Mills), 00:03 (Fullerton), 13:40 (Issaquah), 22:23 the previous evening (Barrington), 16:36 or 17:36 the previous afternoon (Sunol) and 16:49 (Bentonville) [E].
edits.why: Source found by the R7_E9-E12 research agent; see sources/R7_E9-E12_findings.md, R7_E9-E12-03.

edits.old: The TU Graz beam-density study (2025) found that training on *denser* data generalized better across 32–128 beams, with gaps under about 3% for modest density changes [I, arXiv 2503.15087; figures taken from the paper's summary and not re-read from its tables].
edits.new: The TU Graz beam-density study (2025) found that training on *denser* data generalized better across 32–128 beams when detection is scored at the loose 0.4 IoU threshold (§C10.6(i)), and that halving or doubling the beam count at test time (for example from 128 to 64 beams, or from 32 to 64) widened the domain gap by at most about 3 percentage points at the strict 0.7 threshold, against about 12 points for a fourfold change [I, arXiv 2503.15087, Eq. (1), Tables 7–8]. The domain gap is the shortfall in vehicle AP (PV-RCNN++) expressed as a percentage of the AP of the same detector trained on the target data, so the 3 points are a change in a relative gap, not mAP points.

edits.old: The two percentages are therefore not consistent with constant loads of the tabulated sizes, and they should not be rescaled to other loads [E].
edits.new: The two percentages are therefore not consistent with constant loads of the tabulated sizes, and they should not be rescaled to other loads [E]. The paper does not derive them from those loads. Each is extrapolated from one measured drop in battery state of charge over a single 17.71-mile cycle started at 95% charge (10.36% for the bare car, 11.05% with sensing and 11.9% with sensing and compute, its Table III), with the cycle repeated until the battery is depleted, so each includes everything else that differed between the three runs; the paper reports no repeat runs or uncertainties [I]. With the 27 kWh pack that Kia specifies [P], the extra 0.69 and 0.85 points of charge correspond to average battery-side draws of about 310 W and 380 W, against the tabulated 122 W and 325 W [E: $0.0069\times27\ {\rm kWh}/0.597\ {\rm h}\approx0.31$ kW and $0.0085\times27/0.597\approx0.38$ kW, with $2{,}149\ {\rm s}=0.597$ h]. The extrapolation is also not exactly inverse to the charge drops, which alone would give losses of 6.2% and 12.9% ($1-10.36/11.05$ and $1-10.36/11.9$).
